candidate.text:
Most adult piano students come back after twenty years and make the same mistake: they try to play the whole piece, then wonder why nothing improves. I did it. I watched students do it week after week.

The fix is almost boring. Pick one bar that trips you up. Play it slowly three times, eyes on the keys. Stop for the day. It feels like too little. It is not.

Over a month, those small sessions add up. You can play from start to finish. You enjoy practicing again.

Try it tonight with the one bar you always stumble on.

checks.text:
I've been thinking about slow practice—what shifts when you deliberately move slower. Whether it's music, craft, or any skill work, the conventional story is that slowing down lets you notice what speed glosses over.

But I'm curious about something deeper. How does this actually feel? Does the attention you build stay with you when you speed back up? And does it change how you think about the work itself, not just how you execute it?

I think the real tension is between the urge to move forward and the value of staying still for a moment. I'm still figuring out what that balance looks like.

What's your experience with slow practice? Has it shifted something for you?
